subject: Accounting
title: Sherron Watkins and Enron
description: A 60-second lesson on Sherron Watkins and Enron.

hook.text: Sherron Watkins wrote a letter to Enron's CEO warning that the company might 'implode in accounting scandals.'

buildup.text: As vice president of corporate development, Watkins saw the hidden entities and their risks.

discovery.text: She warned Ken Lay directly—but her concerns were dismissed and the fraud continued.

twist.text: Watkins was investigated internally for disloyalty. The fraud wasn't investigated at all.

climax.text: Time magazine named her Person of the Year. Her warning, ignored, proved devastatingly accurate.

punchline.text: She warned them. They investigated her instead.

quiz.question: What happened when Sherron Watkins warned Enron's CEO?
options: Her concerns were dismissed and she was investigated for disloyalty
The CEO immediately fixed the problem
She was promoted for her courage

details.summary: Sherron Watkins was the Enron vice president who warned CEO Ken Lay about the company's fraudulent accounting practices in 2001. This topic tells the story of her memo, the corporate response, and how her actions shaped whistleblower protections.
details.whyItMatters: Watkins' story illustrates both the courage required to challenge powerful executives and the limitations of internal reporting when leadership is complicit in fraud.
takeaways: Watkins wrote a detailed memo to CEO Ken Lay warning of accounting irregularities
Enron's leadership dismissed her concerns and considered firing her instead
Her testimony to Congress was pivotal in passing Sarbanes-Oxley and whistleblower protections

faq.question: What did Sherron Watkins do at Enron?
faq.answer: In August 2001, Watkins wrote a memo to CEO Ken Lay warning that Enron's off-balance-sheet partnerships were hiding billions in debt and could cause the company to implode. Despite her warnings, leadership took no corrective action.

faq.question: Did Sherron Watkins receive whistleblower protection?
faq.answer: Watkins reported internally, not to authorities, so existing whistleblower laws didn't fully apply. Her experience helped inspire the whistleblower protections in the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, which protects employees who report fraud to the SEC.
